report:
## Conclusion

Based on the best available evidence, **saw palmetto (Serenoa repens) preparations do not meaningfully improve symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) compared to placebo over the longer term.**

The most rigorous trials and systematic reviews converge on this conclusion:

- **The Cochrane systematic review** (Tacklind et al.) concluded that Serenoa repens, even at double and triple the usual dose, did not improve urinary flow measures or prostate size in men with lower urinary tract symptoms consistent with BPH. Adverse events were mild and comparable to placebo. ([Cochrane Library](https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD002281.pub3/full))

- **The STEP trial** (NEJM, 2006), a one-year randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 225 men, found that saw palmetto was **not superior to placebo** for improving urinary symptoms or objective measures of BPH. ([NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053085))

- **The CAMUS trial** (Barry et al., JAMA 2011), an 18-month NIH-funded trial escalating doses up to 960 mg/day, also found **no significant benefit** over placebo for urinary symptoms. ([PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3716255/))

- A 2024 AAFP evidence summary states that saw palmetto, alone or in combination, **does not improve urologic symptoms or quality of life** in either the short term (3–6 months) or long term (12–17 months). ([AAFP](https://www.aafp.org/afp/2024/0500/cochrane-saw-palmetto-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia))

While some older or smaller studies suggested modest benefits, the high-quality, longer-term, placebo-controlled evidence—including the largest and most rigorous trials—shows no clinically meaningful improvement. Saw palmetto appears safe and well tolerated, but it should not be relied upon as an effective treatment for BPH symptoms.
